investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Define sensitivity and give its formula.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN). It is the proportion of people WITH the disease who test positive (the detection rate). A highly sensitive test has few false negatives.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Define specificity and give its formula.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP). It is the proportion of people WITHOUT the disease who test negative. A highly specific test has few false positives.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: What do the mnemonics SnNOut and SpPIn mean?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: SnNOut: a highly Sensitive test that is Negative rules the disease OUT. SpPIn: a highly Specific test that is Positive rules the disease IN.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: How does lowering the positivity cut-off affect sensitivity and specificity?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Lowering the threshold raises sensitivity (catches more true cases, fewer false negatives) but lowers specificity (more false positives). It is a trade-off shown by the ROC curve.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: What does the ROC AUC tell you, and what values are meaningful?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: The area under the ROC curve summarises overall discrimination. AUC near 1.0 = excellent discrimination; AUC of 0.5 = no better than chance (useless test).

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: How do parallel and serial testing strategies affect net sensitivity and specificity?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Parallel testing (positive if either test is positive) raises net sensitivity (better for ruling out). Serial testing (positive only if both are positive) raises net specificity (better for ruling in).

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Define positive predictive value (PPV) and give its formula.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: PPV = TP/(TP+FP). It is the probability that a person with a POSITIVE test truly has the disease.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Define negative predictive value (NPV) and give its formula.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: NPV = TN/(TN+FN). It is the probability that a person with a NEGATIVE test truly is disease-free.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Which test characteristics depend on prevalence and which do not?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: PPV and NPV depend on prevalence (pre-test probability). Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic to the test and do NOT change with prevalence.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: As prevalence rises, what happens to PPV and NPV for a fixed test?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: PPV increases and NPV decreases.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Why does screening a low-prevalence population produce so many false positives?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: With few truly diseased people, even a small false-positive rate applied to the large well population outnumbers the true positives, so PPV falls and most positives are false alarms.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: A screening test is positive in a low-prevalence population — what should you do, and what do you tell the patient?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Because PPV is low, treat it as provisional and confirm with a definitive diagnostic test before diagnosis/treatment. Counsel that a positive screen is not a diagnosis and most positives in this setting are false.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: How is a negative test used in a low-prevalence setting?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: NPV is very high, so a negative result reliably excludes disease and permits reassurance/discharge without further testing.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Formula for LR+ (positive likelihood ratio)?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity). It measures how much a positive test result raises the odds of disease. LR+ > 10 is strong evidence to rule the disease IN.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Formula for LR− (negative likelihood ratio)?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity. It measures how much a negative result lowers the odds of disease. LR− < 0.1 is strong evidence to rule the disease OUT.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Why are likelihood ratios superior to predictive values?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: LRs are properties of the test itself and are INDEPENDENT of prevalence, whereas PPV and NPV change with the prevalence of disease in the tested population.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: How do you use an LR to update disease probability?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Pre-test odds × LR = post-test odds. Convert probability to odds [odds = p/(1−p)], multiply by the LR, then convert back [p = odds/(1+odds)]. The Fagan nomogram does this graphically.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: What do SpPIn and SnNOut mean?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: SpPIn: a Specific test with a Positive result rules the disease IN (high LR+). SnNOut: a Sensitive test with a Negative result rules the disease OUT (low LR−).

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Give the full likelihood-ratio interpretation ladder.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: LR+: >10 large, 5–10 moderate, 2–5 small (rule-in). LR−: <0.1 large, 0.1–0.2 moderate, 0.2–0.5 small (rule-out). LR ~0.5–2 = negligible shift; LR = 1 useless.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: What is the bedside (nomogram-free) rule for how much an LR shifts probability?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: McGee’s rule: LRs of 2/5/10 add roughly +15/+30/+45 percentage points; LRs of 0.5/0.2/0.1 subtract ~15/30/45 points (in the mid-probability range).

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Why are multi-level (stratum-specific) likelihood ratios more useful than a single cut-off?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Each result band has its own LR, so a strongly positive result shifts probability far more than a weakly positive one. Dichotomising a graded test (e.g. D-dimer level, troponin band) discards this information — an advantage LR has over sens/spec/PPV.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: What is the purpose of screening, and how does it differ from diagnosis?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Screening tests an apparently healthy, asymptomatic population to identify those at higher risk of a disease or its precursor, so earlier intervention improves outcomes. It is not diagnostic: a positive screen selects people for a definitive diagnostic test, not for treatment.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: List the four Wilson & Jungner domains and their core requirement.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: CONDITION: important problem with a recognisable latent stage and understood natural history. TEST: simple, safe, acceptable, valid with an agreed cut-off. TREATMENT: an accepted effective treatment exists and early treatment beats late. PROGRAMME: cost-effective, continuous, with adequate facilities and an agreed policy on whom to treat.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Define lead-time bias.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Earlier detection by screening moves the diagnosis date forward, lengthening measured survival from diagnosis even when the actual date of death is unchanged. It makes screen-detected survival look falsely better without anyone living longer.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Define length-time bias.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Screening preferentially detects slow-growing, indolent disease with a long pre-clinical phase and inherently better prognosis, while aggressive fast-growing disease surfaces symptomatically between screens. This overstates the apparent benefit of screening.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Give the UK adult and infant screening programmes with their targets.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Cervical (hrHPV, women 25-64), breast (mammography, 50-71, 3-yearly), bowel (FIT, 50-74, 2-yearly), AAA (one-off ultrasound, men at 65), antenatal (infections, Down's, anomaly scan) and newborn bloodspot (day 5 heel-prick for CF, congenital hypothyroidism, sickle cell and other conditions).

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Which body decides UK screening programmes, and against what?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: The UK National Screening Committee (NSC) appraises evidence against modernised Wilson–Jungner criteria (RCT benefit, cost-effectiveness, acceptable harm–benefit) and advises the four UK governments whether to introduce, modify or stop a programme.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Why does screening require informed choice?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Because it invites well people and carries real harms (false positives, overdiagnosis, overtreatment); participants must understand benefits and harms and may decline.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Name the three UK newborn screening programmes.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Bloodspot (day 5, 9 conditions), newborn hearing (OAE ± AABR), and NIPE (physical examination at 72 h and 6–8 weeks).

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: What triggers the legal duty to notify a notifiable disease in the UK?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Reasonable CLINICAL SUSPICION of the disease by the attending registered medical practitioner. You must notify promptly without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: To whom is a notifiable disease reported, and how quickly?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: To the proper officer of the local authority / UKHSA. Urgent cases (e.g. meningococcal disease, diphtheria, VHF) same day by phone; routine cases in writing within 3 days.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Name six common notifiable diseases in the UK.
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Measles, mumps, rubella, meningococcal disease/meningitis, TB, cholera, diphtheria, whooping cough (pertussis), food poisoning, acute infectious hepatitis, HUS, malaria, rabies, viral haemorrhagic fever, COVID-19 (any six).

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Is HIV a statutorily notifiable disease in the UK?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: No. HIV is NOT on the statutory notifiable list (patient confidentiality); it is monitored through confidential voluntary surveillance instead.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: What is the public-health purpose of prompt notification?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: To enable contact tracing, prophylaxis of contacts, early outbreak detection, and outbreak control before further spread occurs. Diagnostic laboratories must separately report notifiable causative organisms.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Which common infections are NOT statutorily notifiable in England?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: HIV, seasonal influenza, Lyme disease, MRSA, C. difficile and the common cold — the classic exam traps. But note the April 2025 changes: chickenpox (varicella), CJD, congenital syphilis and disseminated gonococcal infection all BECAME notifiable, so chickenpox is no longer a valid 'not notifiable' answer.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: Does statutory notification of a notifiable disease need the patient’s consent?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: No — it is a lawful public-interest/statutory disclosure that overrides the usual duty of confidentiality; you notify even if the patient objects. (HIV is kept confidential precisely because it is non-statutory.)

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.front: What follows notification of suspected meningococcal disease?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.back: Notify same day by phone; UKHSA arranges single-dose ciprofloxacin (or rifampicin) prophylaxis for close/household contacts.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A test is evaluated against a gold standard. Among 200 people who truly have the disease, 180 test positive and 20 test negative. What is the sensitivity of the test?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) = 180 / (180 + 20) = 180/200 = 90%. It measures the proportion of truly diseased people the test correctly identifies as positive.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A GP wants a test to help safely rule OUT deep vein thrombosis in a low-risk patient so that further imaging can be avoided. Which test property is most desirable for this purpose?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: A highly sensitive test has few false negatives, so a negative result reliably rules the disease out (SnNOut). This is why a sensitive D-dimer is used to exclude DVT in low-risk patients.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: Which statement about sensitivity, specificity and predictive values is correct?
options: Sensitivity increases as disease prevalence rises
Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic properties of the test and broadly independent of prevalence
Positive predictive value is independent of prevalence
Specificity is calculated as TP / (TP + FP)
Lowering the cut-off increases both sensitivity and specificity
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.answer: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic properties of the test and broadly independent of prevalence
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are calculated down the columns of the 2x2 table by true disease status, so they describe the test itself and are broadly stable across populations. Predictive values, by contrast, depend on prevalence.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: In a 2×2 table, a test gives TP=80, FP=30, FN=20, TN=270. What is the specificity?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) = 270/(270+30) = 270/300 = 90%. The trap answer TP/(TP+FP) = 80/110 ≈ 73% is the positive predictive value, not specificity.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A test with fixed sensitivity and specificity is used first in a symptomatic hospital clinic and later in a general-public screening programme. Compared with the clinic, what happens to the PPV in the screening setting?
options: PPV rises because prevalence is lower
PPV is unchanged because it is intrinsic to the test
PPV falls because prevalence is lower
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.answer: PPV falls because prevalence is lower
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: PPV depends on pre-test probability, which is lower in a screening population. With fewer true cases, false positives dominate the positive results, so PPV falls even though the test itself is unchanged.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A test has sensitivity 99% and specificity 95%. Applied to 100,000 people with a disease prevalence of 0.1%, roughly what is the PPV?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Of 100 diseased people, ~99 are true positives; of 99,900 well people, ~4,995 are false positives. PPV = 99/(99+4995), which is roughly 2%, so most positives are false.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: Which statement about predictive values is correct?
options: PPV and NPV are independent of prevalence, whereas sensitivity and specificity are not
Sensitivity and specificity are independent of prevalence, whereas PPV and NPV are not
All four measures rise as prevalence rises
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.answer: Sensitivity and specificity are independent of prevalence, whereas PPV and NPV are not
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic properties measured down the disease columns and do not change with prevalence. PPV and NPV combine test accuracy with pre-test probability, so they shift as prevalence changes.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A widely-used screening test has 99% sensitivity and 98% specificity and is applied to a low-prevalence population. A patient tests NEGATIVE. What is the best interpretation?
options: The negative result is unreliable because prevalence is low
A confirmatory test is mandatory before excluding disease
The result cannot be interpreted without the likelihood ratio
The high NPV means disease is reliably excluded — reassure
Specificity determines the negative predictive value directly
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.answer: The high NPV means disease is reliably excluded — reassure
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: In a low-prevalence population NPV is very high, so a negative result reliably excludes disease and supports reassurance/discharge. (By contrast a POSITIVE result would have low PPV and need confirmation.)

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A new diagnostic test has a sensitivity of 0.90 and a specificity of 0.95. What is its positive likelihood ratio (LR+)?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) = 0.90 / (1 − 0.95) = 0.90 / 0.05 = 18. A value of 18 exceeds 10, so a positive result is strong evidence to rule the disease in.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A test has a sensitivity of 0.80 and a specificity of 0.50. What is its negative likelihood ratio (LR−)?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity = (1 − 0.80) / 0.50 = 0.20 / 0.50 = 0.40. As this is well above 0.1, a negative result only modestly lowers the odds of disease.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A patient has a pre-test probability of disease of 20%. A test with an LR+ of 6 returns positive. What is the approximate post-test probability?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Pre-test odds = 0.20 / 0.80 = 0.25; post-test odds = 0.25 × 6 = 1.5; post-test probability = 1.5 / (1 + 1.5) = 0.6, i.e. 60%. This demonstrates converting probability to odds, applying the LR, and converting back.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A diagnostic test result carries a positive likelihood ratio of 3. How should this be interpreted?
options: A large, near-diagnostic increase in probability
A small increase in probability that often does not cross a decision threshold
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.answer: A small increase in probability that often does not cross a decision threshold
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: An LR+ of 2–5 produces only a small shift in probability (roughly +15–20 points mid-range) and frequently does not cross a clinical decision threshold — LR+ needs to be >10 for a large, near-diagnostic rule-in.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A new blood test is proposed to screen the general population for a rare cancer. Which single feature is MOST essential before a national screening programme is introduced, according to Wilson & Jungner?
options: The test is inexpensive to manufacture
The disease is frequently discussed in the media
An accepted, effective treatment exists and treating the early stage improves outcome more than treating late
The test can be performed at home
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.answer: An accepted, effective treatment exists and treating the early stage improves outcome more than treating late
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Screening is only worthwhile if earlier detection changes outcome, which requires an accepted effective treatment that works better in the latent or early stage. Without this, early detection merely lengthens the time a person knows they are ill.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A cancer screening programme reports that 5-year survival from diagnosis is much higher in screen-detected patients than in those diagnosed after symptoms, yet a randomised trial shows no reduction in disease-specific mortality. Which bias best explains this discrepancy?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Lead-time bias arises because screening advances the date of diagnosis, so survival measured from diagnosis appears longer even when the date of death is unchanged. This is why programme benefit is judged by mortality in randomised trials rather than survival from detection.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: Which statement about UK national screening programmes is correct?
options: Bowel cancer screening uses annual colonoscopy for everyone over 40
Abdominal aortic aneurysm screening offers a one-off ultrasound to men at age 65
Breast screening uses MRI for all women from age 30
Cervical screening treats women directly on the basis of the screening result
Newborn bloodspot screening is performed within one hour of birth
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.answer: Abdominal aortic aneurysm screening offers a one-off ultrasound to men at age 65
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: The UK AAA programme invites men in their 65th year for a single abdominal ultrasound, as aneurysm risk rises with age in men. The other options misstate the modality, age range, or the principle that a positive screen leads to diagnostic follow-up rather than direct treatment.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: Which organisation advises the UK governments on whether to introduce or stop a national screening programme?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: The UK National Screening Committee appraises the evidence against modernised Wilson–Jungner criteria and recommends to the four UK governments whether to introduce, modify or stop a screening programme.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A GP sees a 6-year-old with fever, coryza, conjunctivitis and a spreading maculopapular rash with Koplik spots, strongly suggesting measles. What is the correct action regarding notification?
options: Await positive measles IgM before notifying, to avoid false alarms
No notification is required as measles is now rare in the UK
Notify the proper officer promptly on clinical suspicion, without waiting for serology
Notify only if a second case appears in the same school
Refer to the hospital and let the admitting team decide on notification
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.answer: Notify the proper officer promptly on clinical suspicion, without waiting for serology
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Measles is a notifiable disease and the statutory duty is triggered by clinical suspicion, not laboratory confirmation. Prompt notification allows contact tracing and prophylaxis before laboratory results become available.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: Which of the following is NOT a statutorily notifiable disease in the UK?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: HIV is deliberately excluded from the statutory notifiable list to protect patient confidentiality, being tracked instead through voluntary confidential surveillance. Tuberculosis, meningococcal disease, cholera and acute infectious hepatitis are all statutorily notifiable.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: Who holds the legal responsibility to notify, and to whom is the notification made?
options: The receptionist notifies the General Medical Council
The attending registered medical practitioner notifies the proper officer of the local authority / UKHSA
The patient self-reports to their employer
The pharmacist notifies the Care Quality Commission
Only the diagnostic laboratory notifies, and only after confirmation
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.answer: The attending registered medical practitioner notifies the proper officer of the local authority / UKHSA
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: The statutory duty rests with the attending registered medical practitioner, who reports to the proper officer of the local authority working with UKHSA. Diagnostic laboratories have a separate parallel duty to report notifiable causative organisms.

investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.question: A GP wants to know which of these is NOT a statutorily notifiable disease in England. Which is correct?
investigations__EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRE.explanation: Seasonal influenza is not statutorily notifiable (nor are HIV, Lyme disease or the common cold) — but influenza of ZOONOTIC origin is, and chickenpox is now notifiable too. Measles, TB, meningococcal disease and food poisoning are all on the notifiable list and must be reported on clinical suspicion.
